note: All five NASA hazards apply to every mission. The order per mission is AstroLife's presentation choice, backed by the cited NASA statements. It is not a NASA ranking, not a probability, and it never changes assessment findings.

radiation.summary: Ionizing radiation from galactic cosmic rays and solar storms. It cannot be seen or felt.
radiation.why_it_matters: NASA describes radiation exposure as increasing cancer risk and as one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight.
observations: Following the shelter procedure when an alert is active
radiation.limits: AstroLife does not measure radiation. A fingertip sensor cannot detect dose.

isolation.summary: Living and working with a small group in a confined space for a long time.
isolation.why_it_matters: NASA notes behavioral responses in isolated, confined groups; crews are selected, trained and supported to work as a team for months or years.
isolation.limits: Self-reports are observations, not a mental-health assessment.

distance.summary: Instructions, supplies and medical care become harder to receive from Earth the farther a crew travels.
distance.why_it_matters: Crews need planning and self-sufficiency, including handling medical events with limited support from Earth.
observations: Any concern you would normally raise with the medical team
distance.limits: AstroLife cannot replace the crew medical officer or mission medical procedures.

gravity.summary: The body adjusts to each new gravity level: weightlessness, the Moon, Mars, and Earth again on return.
gravity.why_it_matters: NASA lists muscles, bones, the inner ear and organs as adjusting to new gravitational loads.
observations: Strength, exercise sessions, bone or back pain
gravity.limits: Pulse and oxygen estimates cannot measure bone density, muscle strength or eye changes.

environment.summary: A spacecraft is a closed habitat: temperature, pressure, lighting, noise, microbes and air quality all matter.
environment.why_it_matters: NASA notes that microbes transfer more easily in closed habitats and that stress hormones and the immune system can change.
observations: Cabin air, CO2 or contamination alerts
environment.limits: SpO2 cannot detect elevated cabin CO2 or contamination.

gravity.rationale: NASA says the whole body must adjust to the gravity encountered on the space station, and again on Earth after return.

environment.rationale: NASA notes that micro-organisms transfer more easily from person to person in closed habitats such as the space station.

radiation.rationale: A lunar mission leaves low Earth orbit. NASA describes ionizing radiation outside Earth's protective magnetic field and atmosphere as a serious risk to astronauts.

gravity.rationale: NASA lists the Moon among the new gravity levels the body must adjust to, in addition to the spacecraft and the return to Earth.

distance.rationale: NASA describes a lunar trip as about three days from Earth, so support is farther away than in low Earth orbit.

radiation.rationale: NASA states that outside Earth's protective magnetic field and atmosphere, ionizing radiation will pose a serious risk to astronauts travelling to Mars.

distance.rationale: NASA gives Mars as about 140 million miles from Earth on average, a mission of roughly three years, with a communication delay of up to 20 minutes one way.

isolation.rationale: NASA notes crews must work effectively as a team for months or years in space.

gravity.rationale: NASA says astronauts on Mars would live in three-eighths of Earth's gravity for up to two years.
